--- title: "Maximum likelihood" description: "Name the distribution you think produced the data, and the loss follows: least squares assumes a Normal response, and Poisson regression a Poisson one." order: 4 categories: [optimisation] --- ## Name the distribution and the loss follows [Loss functions](loss-functions.qmd) ended with a table: squared error for a measurement, Poisson deviance for a count, log loss for presence or absence. Those losses are not a list to memorise. Each comes from one principle, **maximum likelihood**: say what kind of distribution you think produced the data, and the loss follows from it. The choice of loss then becomes a question you can answer from the survey: what kind of quantity is the response, and how does it vary? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Likelihood reads probability backwards Probability starts from a model and asks how likely the data are. **Likelihood** starts from the data and asks which parameter values make them most likely. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mu <- seq(0.05, 15, length.out = 400) one <- tibble(mu, likelihood = dpois(3, mu)) |> ggplot(aes(mu, likelihood)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = ml_palette[["blue"]]) + labs(x = "Expected count μ", y = "P(count = 3)", title = "One station, counted 3") counts <- c(3, 0, 11) joint <- tibble(mu, L = dpois(counts[1], mu) * dpois(counts[2], mu) * dpois(counts[3], mu)) three <- map_dfr(counts, \(k) tibble(mu, L = dpois(k, mu), curve = paste("counted", k))) |> ggplot(aes(mu, L)) + geom_line(aes(group = curve), colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.5) + geom_line(data = joint |> mutate(L = L / max(L) * 0.3), colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], linewidth = 1.1) + geom_vline(xintercept = mean(counts), linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]) + labs(x = "Expected count μ", y = "Likelihood", title = "Three stations, and their product") one + three ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![On the left, the Poisson probability of counting exactly 3 animals, for each expected count μ. It peaks at μ = 3. On the right, the same curve for three stations that caught 3, 0 and 11 (grey), and their product (red), rescaled to fit. The product peaks at 4.67, the mean of the three counts, and is narrower than any single curve.](maximum-likelihood_files/figure-html/fig-one-station-1.png){#fig-one-station fig-alt='Two panels. The left panel shows a single humped curve rising from zero at mu equals zero to a peak of about 0.22 at mu equals 3, then falling slowly towards zero by mu equals 15. The right panel shows three thin grey curves peaking near zero, near 3 and near 11, and a taller narrow red curve peaking at 4.7, marked by a dashed line. The red curve is narrower than every grey curve.' width=1500} ::: ::: ::: Take one station where 3 animals were counted, and suppose the counts follow a Poisson distribution with some expected count $\mu$. If $\mu$ were 3, a count of 3 would be quite likely; if $\mu$ were 0.2 or 30, it would be a surprise. Plotting that probability against $\mu$ gives the **likelihood** for that station. With one station, almost any $\mu$ between 1 and 8 is plausible. Stations are independent, so the probability of several counts together is the product of their probabilities. The product is high only where one value of $\mu$ explains all the counts at once, so it is narrower than any single curve, and each extra station narrows it further. The **maximum likelihood estimate** is the value at its peak. ## Taking logs turns the likelihood into a loss The survey has 749 stations with chlorophyll and depth measured. The product of 749 probabilities, each below one, is so small that R stores it as 0. Taking the logarithm turns the product into a sum, which a computer handles easily, and does not move the peak. Fitting algorithms find a lowest point, not a highest one, so they minimise the **negative log-likelihood** instead. That is a loss averaged (or summed) over the data, exactly like the objectives on [Loss functions](loss-functions.qmd). Change the distribution, and the loss changes with it. | If the response is assumed to be… | The negative log-likelihood is… | Used by | | --- | --- | --- | | Normal, with the same spread everywhere | Squared error | Linear regression, `lm()` | | Laplace, a sharper peak with heavier tails | Absolute error | Least absolute deviations | | Poisson | Poisson deviance | Poisson regression | | Negative binomial | Negative binomial deviance | Count regression with extra spread | | Bernoulli, yes or no | Log loss | Logistic regression | ::: {.diagram} ![A distribution for the response gives a loss. A Normal response, a measurement that can take any value with the same spread everywhere, gives squared error. A Poisson response, a count, gives Poisson deviance. A Bernoulli response, presence or absence, gives log loss.](img/distributions-to-losses.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Normal, gives squared error, a measurement that can take any value: a bell curve centred on a dashed line marked prediction, with the part of the curve below a dashed zero line shaded; same spread everywhere, and values below zero allowed. Poisson, gives Poisson deviance, a count of 0, 1, 2 and so on: bars for counts from 0 to 10, highest near 3; whole numbers from zero, with spread growing with the mean. Bernoulli, gives log loss, presence or absence: a short bar for absent and a taller bar for present; one probability of presence, the rest goes to absence. A note says: name the distribution, and its negative log-likelihood is the loss."} ::: The first row matters most. Least squares assumes a Normal response with the same spread everywhere, whether or not anyone says so. A Normal distribution runs below zero, and nothing in squared error objects to a negative prediction, which is why [polynomial regression](../03-supervised-learning/linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd) in section 3 predicted a negative count. Poisson regression names a distribution that stops at zero, and the problem goes away. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The maths, if you want it With $p(y_i \mid \theta)$ the probability of observation $i$ under parameters $\theta$, $$\text{maximise } \sum_i \log p(y_i \mid \theta) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \text{minimise } \sum_i -\log p(y_i \mid \theta)$$ For a Normal response with mean $\hat y_i$ and standard deviation $\sigma$, $$-\log p(y_i \mid \hat y_i, \sigma) = \frac{(y_i - \hat y_i)^2}{2\sigma^2} + \log \sigma + \tfrac{1}{2}\log 2\pi$$ For a fixed $\sigma$, only the first term depends on the predictions, and it is squared error divided by a constant, so the same line minimises both. ::: ## Worked example ### Least squares is the Normal likelihood We fit a line of abundance against standardised chlorophyll twice: once by writing down the Normal negative log-likelihood and minimising it with `optim()`, once with `lm()`. The likelihood never mentions a squared residual. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} X <- model.matrix(~ chl_z, data = d) # The spread sigma is a parameter too. It is searched on the log scale, so the # search cannot propose a negative one. neg_log_lik_normal <- function(par) { -sum(dnorm(y, mean = X %*% par[1:2], sd = exp(par[3]), log = TRUE)) } normal_mle <- optim(c(0, 0, 1), neg_log_lik_normal, method = "BFGS", control = list(reltol = 1e-14, maxit = 5000)) ls_fit <- lm(abundance ~ chl_z, data = d) normal_compare <- tibble( method = c("Maximum likelihood", "Least squares, lm()"), intercept = c(normal_mle$par[1], coef(ls_fit)[1]), slope = c(normal_mle$par[2], coef(ls_fit)[2]), sigma = c(exp(normal_mle$par[3]), sqrt(mean(residuals(ls_fit)^2))) ) normal_compare |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|method | intercept| slope| sigma| |:-------------------|---------:|------:|------:| |Maximum likelihood | 4.008| 1.8238| 4.5013| |Least squares, lm() | 4.008| 1.8238| 4.5013|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.api as sm from scipy.optimize import minimize from scipy.stats import norm, poisson from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, PoissonRegressor from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() def standardise(column): return (column - column.mean()) / column.std() d = survey[["abundance", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "depth_m"]].dropna() d = d.assign(chl_z=standardise(d["chlorophyll_mg_m3"]), depth_z=standardise(d["depth_m"])) y = d["abundance"].to_numpy() X = sm.add_constant(d[["chl_z"]]).to_numpy() # The spread sigma is a parameter too. It is searched on the log scale, so the # search cannot propose a negative one. def neg_log_lik_normal(par): return -norm.logpdf(y, loc=X @ par[:2], scale=np.exp(par[2])).sum() normal_mle = minimize(neg_log_lik_normal, x0=[0, 0, 1], method="BFGS", options={"gtol": 1e-8}) ls_fit = LinearRegression().fit(d[["chl_z"]], y) pd.DataFrame({ "method": ["Maximum likelihood", "Least squares, LinearRegression"], "intercept": [normal_mle.x[0], ls_fit.intercept_], "slope": [normal_mle.x[1], ls_fit.coef_[0]], "sigma": [np.exp(normal_mle.x[2]), np.sqrt(np.mean((y - ls_fit.predict(d[["chl_z"]])) ** 2))], }).round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | method | intercept | slope | sigma | |:--------------------------------|------------:|--------:|--------:| | Maximum likelihood | 4.008 | 1.8238 | 4.5013 | | Least squares, LinearRegression | 4.008 | 1.8238 | 4.5013 | ::: ::: ::: The two agree to the fourth decimal place: asking for the line that makes the counts most likely under a Normal distribution gives the least-squares line. ### Poisson regression is the Poisson likelihood Changing `dnorm` to `dpois`, and passing the weighted sum through $e$ so that the expected count stays above zero, gives Poisson regression. We add depth and its square, as in [Regression for counts](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd). ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Xp <- model.matrix(~ chl_z + depth_z + I(depth_z^2), data = d) neg_log_lik_poisson <- function(b) { -sum(dpois(y, lambda = exp(drop(Xp %*% b)), log = TRUE)) } poisson_mle <- optim(rep(0, ncol(Xp)), neg_log_lik_poisson, method = "BFGS", control = list(reltol = 1e-14, maxit = 5000)) poisson_glm <- glm(abundance ~ chl_z + depth_z + I(depth_z^2), data = d, family = poisson) tibble( term = colnames(Xp), `by optim` = poisson_mle$par, `by glm()` = coef(poisson_glm) ) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 5))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | by optim| by glm()| |:------------|--------:|--------:| |(Intercept) | 1.41315| 1.41315| |chl_z | 0.24063| 0.24063| |depth_z | -0.16657| -0.16657| |I(depth_z^2) | -0.09586| -0.09586|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} Xp = sm.add_constant(d[["chl_z", "depth_z"]].assign(depth_z2=d["depth_z"] ** 2)) def neg_log_lik_poisson(b): return -poisson.logpmf(y, mu=np.exp(Xp.to_numpy() @ b)).sum() poisson_mle = minimize(neg_log_lik_poisson, x0=np.zeros(Xp.shape[1]), method="BFGS", options={"gtol": 1e-8}) poisson_glm = sm.GLM(y, Xp, family=sm.families.Poisson()).fit() # scikit-learn's PoissonRegressor adds a penalty by default (alpha=1.0); # alpha=0 switches it off, and then it fits the same likelihood. poisson_sk = PoissonRegressor(alpha=0, max_iter=1000).fit(Xp.drop(columns="const"), y) pd.DataFrame({ "by minimize": poisson_mle.x, "by statsmodels": poisson_glm.params, "by PoissonRegressor": [poisson_sk.intercept_, *poisson_sk.coef_], }).round(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | | by minimize | by statsmodels | by PoissonRegressor | |:---------|--------------:|-----------------:|----------------------:| | const | 1.41315 | 1.41315 | 1.41314 | | chl_z | 0.24063 | 0.24063 | 0.24063 | | depth_z | -0.16657 | -0.16657 | -0.16656 | | depth_z2 | -0.09586 | -0.09586 | -0.09586 | ::: ::: ::: The coefficients agree to five decimal places, and so do the log-likelihoods: −2492.032 by `optim()` and −2492.032 by `glm()`. `glm(family = poisson)` is this likelihood with a faster search. The standard errors in `glm()`'s summary come from the same curve. A log-likelihood that falls away sharply from its peak means the data rule out nearby values, and the standard error is small; a flat peak means they do not, and it is large. ### Raw units stop the search The search above used standardised inputs. Here it is with depth in metres, so that depth squared runs into the thousands. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Xraw <- model.matrix(~ chlorophyll_mg_m3 + depth_m + I(depth_m^2), data = d) raw_mle <- optim(rep(0, ncol(Xraw)), \(b) -sum(dpois(y, lambda = exp(drop(Xraw %*% b)), log = TRUE)), method = "BFGS", control = list(reltol = 1e-14, maxit = 5000)) signif(raw_mle$par, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 1.3e-31 3.0e-31 9.5e-30 -8.0e-16 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} raw_mle$convergence ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 0 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} Xraw = sm.add_constant(d[["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "depth_m"]] .assign(depth_m2=d["depth_m"] ** 2)).to_numpy() # scipy's search also fails here, but differently: its first step is so large # that exp() overflows, and it reports failure where optim() reports success. with np.errstate(over="ignore", invalid="ignore"): raw_mle = minimize(lambda b: -poisson.logpmf(y, mu=np.exp(Xraw @ b)).sum(), x0=np.zeros(Xraw.shape[1]), method="BFGS") print("coefficients:", np.array2string(raw_mle.x, precision=2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> coefficients: [1.46e-01 3.49e-01 1.10e+01 1.03e+03] ``` ::: ```{.python .cell-code} print("success:", raw_mle.success) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> success: False ``` ::: ```{.python .cell-code} print("message:", raw_mle.message) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> message: Desired error not necessarily achieved due to precision loss. ``` ::: ::: ::: The coefficients are still zero, where the search started, and a convergence code of 0 means `optim()` reports success. The search gives up at the first step, and nothing in the output says so. It is the problem from [Gradient descent](gradient-descent.qmd): inputs on very different scales make a search fail. `glm()` fits the raw inputs without trouble, because its search, the one written out on [Finding the parameters](parameter-estimation.qmd), handles scale differently. [Finding the parameters](parameter-estimation.qmd#each-sign-of-a-failed-search-has-its-own-fix) shows how to catch a search that stops like this. ### The negative binomial model adds one parameter ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dispersion <- deviance(poisson_glm) / df.residual(poisson_glm) nb_fit <- MASS::glm.nb(abundance ~ chl_z + depth_z + I(depth_z^2), data = d) tibble( model = c("Poisson regression", "Negative binomial model"), parameters = c(length(coef(poisson_glm)), length(coef(nb_fit)) + 1), `log-likelihood` = c(as.numeric(logLik(poisson_glm)), as.numeric(logLik(nb_fit))), theta = c("none", format(round(nb_fit$theta, 2))) ) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | parameters| log-likelihood|theta | |:-----------------------|----------:|--------------:|:-----| |Poisson regression | 4| -2492.03|none | |Negative binomial model | 5| -1828.43|1.06 |
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} dispersion = poisson_glm.deviance / poisson_glm.df_resid # statsmodels estimates alpha = 1 / theta, the extra spread the other way round. nb_fit = sm.NegativeBinomial(y, Xp).fit(method="newton", disp=0) pd.DataFrame({ "model": ["Poisson regression", "Negative binomial model"], "parameters": [len(poisson_glm.params), len(nb_fit.params)], "log-likelihood": [poisson_glm.llf, nb_fit.llf], "theta": ["none", f"{1 / nb_fit.params['alpha']:.2f}"], }).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | parameters | log-likelihood | theta | |:------------------------|-------------:|-----------------:|:--------| | Poisson regression | 4 | -2492.03 | none | | Negative binomial model | 5 | -1828.43 | 1.06 | ::: ::: ::: These counts vary more than Poisson allows: the deviance is 4.2 times its degrees of freedom, where Poisson expects about 1. [Regression for counts](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd) called this overdispersion. The negative binomial model adds one parameter, $\theta$, for the extra spread, and `glm.nb()` estimates it by maximum likelihood along with the coefficients: $\theta$ = 1.06. That one parameter raises the log-likelihood from −2492 to −1828. The coefficients change little, but the Poisson standard errors are only 32% to 49% of the negative binomial model's: under the wrong distribution, the model was far more sure of itself than the data allow. Two cautions come with these numbers. $\theta$ describes the spread left over *given the inputs in the model*, so adding an input changes it. And log-likelihoods can be compared only between models of the same response: a model of `abundance` and one of `log(abundance + 1)` give likelihoods of different quantities. ## Forests and boosting have no likelihood A random forest or a boosted model states no distribution for the response, so it has no likelihood: no log-likelihood to compare and no standard errors from the curve's shape. That is part of the trade in [Choosing a method](../03-supervised-learning/choosing-a-method.qmd): the flexible methods give up these tools in exchange for fitting any shape. Maximum likelihood also has a weakness of its own. It finds the parameters that make *this* dataset most likely, and with many parameters and few stations those fit the noise as well as the pattern. [Priors and ridge regression](map-and-priors.qmd) adds a preference for small parameters to the likelihood to hold them back. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - **Likelihood** is the probability of the data at given parameter values; the **maximum likelihood estimate** is the value that makes the data most likely. - The negative log-likelihood is a loss. Name the distribution, and the loss follows: Normal gives squared error, Poisson gives Poisson deviance, Bernoulli gives log loss. - Least squares assumes a Normal response, which is why it allows negative counts. - Writing the likelihood by hand reproduced `lm()` and `glm()`; with inputs in raw units the same search stopped at its start and reported success. - One dispersion parameter raised the log-likelihood from −2492 to −1828, and the Poisson standard errors were 32% to 49% of the negative binomial model's. - Forests and boosting have no likelihood, and so no standard errors of this kind. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. The negative log-likelihood of a Laplace distribution with spread $s$ is `sum(abs(y - mu)) / s + length(y) * log(2 * s)`. Fit a line of abundance against `chlorophyll_mg_m3` by minimising it with `optim()`, and compare the intercept and slope with the absolute-error line on [Loss functions](loss-functions.qmd). 2. Add `temperature_c` to the negative binomial model and refit. Does $\theta$ go up or down, and what does that say about where some of the extra spread came from?
